problem: MLLM-based VLN methods use next-step action imitation that supervises only the expert action and needs large data, and they maintain state via cognitive maps, dense/uniformly-sampled history frames or external 3D tools (e.g. VGGT), which costs GPU memory and time and can miss key events.
motivation: Efficient VLN needs both data-efficient supervision and memory management that keeps navigation-critical history. Language labels derived automatically from expert trajectories can supply richer supervision, and the model itself can decide which frames to remember.
key_idea: Train an MLLM to autoregressively output, in language tags, navigation progress, a future-outcome label for each candidate action, and a memory keep/drop decision with a semantic role, before the final action, with the kept frames stored in a bounded FIFO memory.
insight: Rule-derived structured language supervision (progress, counterfactual outcomes, memory roles) extracts more from the same expert data: removing LFS drops SR from 49.7 to 46.9, and action-only IL gets 41.7. Learned event-driven memory matters more than sampling: swapping in JanusVLN's uniform sampling at inference without retraining drops SR to 37.4, while OS rises to 70.9, which suggests LFS steers toward the goal and EDRM supports stopping. Memory stays bounded (<24GB, 59ms/step), so cost is lower than JanusVLN's.
method: Language Centric Future State Modeling (LFS): the MLLM outputs <Progress> (one of 5 coarse labels) and <Outcome> (one of 16 outcome labels for each candidate action in MOVE/TURN_LEFT/TURN_RIGHT/STOP) before the action, so the action is conditioned on explicit consequence reasoning.

Event Driven Rolling Memory (EDRM): at each step the model emits <MemoryWrite> keep/drop and <MemoryRole> (7 roles, e.g. turn_start, turn_end, stop_evidence); kept frames go into a FIFO queue (length 8) and dropped frames stay only as recent context.
Unified structured target and loss: a single sequence (p, F, W, R, action) is trained with standard next-token NLL, with no auxiliary loss or heuristic.

Deterministic label construction: labels are built from expert trajectories with a K=5 future-action window; non-expert candidate actions get rule-based counterfactual outcome labels (too_early, wrong_turn, over_turn, etc.) with no extra rollouts; progress is derived from t/(T-1).
Oracle information-theoretic motivation: H(a|X)-H(a|X,F*)=I(a;F*|X)>=0, plus a bound eps_actual<=eps_oracle+delta covering the generation-error gap.
Backbone and training: Qwen3-VL 8B fine-tuned for 1 epoch on R2R-CE and RxR-CE only with ms-swift (lr 1e-5, 8xA100, ~1000 GPU hours), monocular RGB input.

setting.training_data: R2R-CE + RxR-CE expert trajectories only (0K extra data, no DAgger); labels auto-generated by rules

results: With only monocular RGB and 0K extra data, LookStep reaches 49.7 SR / 45.3 SPL on R2R-CE val-unseen (above StreamVLN* 45.5 SR and Uni-NaVid 47.0 SR, equal to NaVILA* 49.7 SR) and 46.9 SR on RxR-CE, but stays below JanusVLN (52.8 SR, 49.2 SPL). Compared with JanusVLN it uses about half the peak GPU memory (<24GB vs 44.3GB) and about a quarter of the inference time (59ms vs 194ms per step).
limitations: Trained only on offline R2R/RxR expert data, with no DAgger or larger data, so it trails JanusVLN and large-scale methods; RxR-CE is also below several baselines.
Failure cases include confusing visually similar landmarks and misjudging the stopping position (scale misestimation); goal_approach memory-role accuracy is only 43.64%.
The theoretical motivation is oracle-level only, and the counterfactual labels are rule-based rather than from real rollouts; the real-world test is small (30 trials).
